blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
At executive level, inbound and outbound flows are not internal processes — they are ecosystems of partners, each running their own business while being expected to move in step with ours. Suppliers, carriers, cross-dock operators and final-mile providers each have their own priorities, their own capacity constraints, and their own set of competitors also making demands on their attention.

The senior leader's job is not to own this ecosystem, which is impossible, but to make the company worth showing up for. That means paying on time, sharing honest forecasts, recognising good work, and being the customer others actually want to keep in their portfolio.

Rarely does tight control produce a resilient ecosystem. Not only does it corrode trust, but it also trains partners to hide bad news — the single most expensive failure mode in logistics. The ecosystems that survive shocks are almost always the ones where bad news travelled upstream early, and the response was coordinated before the public even noticed.

items.q: According to the text, how should inbound and outbound flows be understood at executive level?
items.why: "they are ecosystems of partners, each running their own business."

items.q: What is described as the senior leader's actual job?
options: To own and control the whole ecosystem
To replace partners who make demands
To make the company worth showing up for
items.why: "not to own this ecosystem… but to make the company worth showing up for."

items.q: The text calls which behaviour "the single most expensive failure mode in logistics"?
items.why: "it also trains partners to hide bad news — the single most expensive failure mode."

items.q: Which statement would the author most likely DISAGREE with?
options: Partners have priorities that compete with ours
Trust makes partners more willing to surface problems
Tight control is the surest route to a resilient ecosystem
Being a customer others want to keep pays off in a crisis
items.why: Inferência: "Rarely does tight control produce a resilient ecosystem" — o texto argumenta o oposto.

items.q: The phrase "before the public even noticed" suggests that…
options: shocks are impossible to survive once they occur
resilient ecosystems contain shocks early enough to avoid visible damage
the public is always the first to detect a logistics failure
partners should conceal problems from customers
items.why: Inferência: quando a má notícia sobe cedo e a resposta é coordenada, o problema é resolvido antes de estourar publicamente.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Oliver reabrindo a conversa com uma das transportadoras. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
Thanks for taking the meeting, Priya — I know the last twelve months haven't given you many reasons to. I'll be honest with you: we negotiated hard, we squeezed every point we could, and somewhere along the way you quietly moved us down your list. I understand why. When capacity got tight last winter, we were the account you deprioritised, and frankly, on the numbers alone, you were right to.

So I'm not here to reopen the rate card today. I'm here to reset how we work. What I want is simple: honest forecasts from us, no more surprise volume dumped on you at midnight, and payment on the terms we agreed — not thirty days after. In return, I'm asking for one thing that money can't buy. When something is about to go wrong, I want to hear it from you early, not discover it downstream when a customer is already shouting.

We can't own your business and we shouldn't try. But I'd like us to be the customer you'd actually fight to keep. If that means less margin for me this year and a partner who moves in step when the next shock lands, I'll take that trade every time.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: Why does Oliver say the carrier moved his account down their list?
options: Because his forecasts were always inflated
Because he negotiated hard and squeezed every point
Because his company changed carriers without notice
Because a competitor offered lower rates
items.why: "we negotiated hard, we squeezed every point we could, and somewhere along the way you quietly moved us down your list."

items.q: What does Oliver say he is NOT there to do today?
items.why: "I'm not here to reopen the rate card today. I'm here to reset how we work."

items.q: What is the one thing Oliver says money can't buy?
options: Early warning when something is about to go wrong
items.why: "When something is about to go wrong, I want to hear it from you early."

items.q: What does Oliver imply by "discover it downstream when a customer is already shouting"?
options: Downstream teams are more reliable than carriers
Hidden problems surface later and more expensively
The carrier should escalate every issue to the customer
Customers should never be told about delays
items.why: Inferência: a má notícia escondida a montante reaparece a jusante, quando já é tarde e cara.

items.q: How would you best describe Oliver's approach in this meeting?
options: Candid, accepting less margin for a partner who stays in step
Purely transactional, focused only on price
Defensive and unwilling to admit fault
items.why: Inferência: ele reconhece o próprio erro e aceita menos margem em troca de sintonia — postura franca, não transacional.

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "Our carriers need to move in step with our release schedule." To move in step means to…
items.why: Move in step = mover-se em sintonia, de forma coordenada.

items.q: Choose the correct term: "A ___ at the port meant the carrier simply had no trucks to spare that week."
items.why: Capacity constraint = restrição de capacidade, o limite físico de recursos disponíveis.

items.q: "Squeezing a partner year after year will slowly corrode the relationship." To corrode means to…
items.why: Corrode = corroer, desgastar aos poucos.

items.q: Upstream, in this supply-chain context, refers to…
options: the direction closer to suppliers and the source
the final-mile delivery to the customer
items.why: Upstream = a montante, mais perto da origem/fornecedores; downstream é a jusante, perto do cliente.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "Mapping every ___ across both flows tells us exactly where the system is most likely to break."
items.why: Failure mode = modo de falha, a forma específica pela qual algo pode quebrar.

blocks.instruction: Expressões que aparecem em conversas de gestão de fornecedores. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "When capacity tightened, the carrier deprioritised our account." This means they…
items.why: Deprioritise = rebaixar na lista de prioridades, atender depois dos outros.

items.q: "We need our best carriers to show up for us when the next shock lands." To show up for someone means to…
options: be reliably present and supportive when it matters
items.why: Show up for = estar presente e apoiar de fato quando importa.

items.q: "If we follow through on the payment terms, trust rebuilds itself." To follow through means to…
items.why: Follow through = cumprir até o fim o que foi combinado.

items.q: "Being the account others want to keep in their portfolio is worth more than a lower rate." A portfolio here is…
options: the set of customers or clients a partner serves
items.why: Portfolio = carteira, o conjunto de clientes que o parceiro atende e mantém.

items.q: "A hard-edged rate cut may save money now, but it won't move the needle on resilience." This means it will…
items.why: Move the needle = mexer o ponteiro, produzir diferença perceptível.
